stem: Which stage of the five-stage RISC pipeline writes the result to a register?
explanation: The stages are IF, ID, EX, MEM and WB.
source: CSC 313-Computer Organization and Architecture.pdf (course material, T. Oguntunde), Unit 11

stem: For a k-stage pipeline running n instructions, the pipelined time is
explanation: The non-pipelined time is n × k × Tp.
source: CSC 313-Computer Organization and Architecture.pdf (course material, T. Oguntunde), Unit 11

stem: In a non-uniform delay pipeline, the cycle time equals the maximum stage delay.
explanation: Stages of 2, 8, 3 and 10 ns give Tp = 10 ns.
source: CSC 313-Computer Organization and Architecture.pdf (course material, T. Oguntunde), Unit 12a

stem: ADD R3 ← R1, R2 followed by SUB R4 ← R3, R1 is which hazard?
explanation: SUB reads R3 before ADD has written it.
source: CSC 313-Computer Organization and Architecture.pdf (course material, T. Oguntunde), Unit 11; 2020/21 paper

stem: Which are types of pipeline hazard (dependency)?
explanation: They introduce stalls in the pipeline.
source: CSC 313-Computer Organization and Architecture.pdf (course material, T. Oguntunde), Unit 11

stem: Which one does not reduce pipeline stalls?
explanation: Interface registers are needed between stages.
source: CSC 313-Computer Organization and Architecture.pdf (course material, T. Oguntunde), Unit 11

stem: Dividing the pipeline into more, shorter stages is
explanation: Superscalar uses several pipelines in parallel.
source: CSC 313-Computer Organization and Architecture.pdf (course material, T. Oguntunde), Unit 13

stem: The speedup of a pipeline can grow without limit as more instructions run.
explanation: It approaches k, the number of stages.
source: CSC 313-Computer Organization and Architecture.pdf (course material, T. Oguntunde), Unit 11
